Here’s the rational framework — think of it as your financial compass, not a magic bullet. You have high-cost debt (19%) and $3,000 in cash. That’s your starting point. The core principle: don’t invest until you’ve neutralized the biggest drag on your wealth.

19% interest on credit card debt is a guaranteed, tax-free, risk-free return you get just by paying it off. No stock, ETF, or crypto can reliably beat that without taking serious risk. Even if you believe the market will return 7–8% annually, why gamble with $3,000 when you can lock in 19% right now?

Your move: use the full $3,000 to pay down the credit card. That’s not ‘saving’ — that’s earning. Every dollar you pay now saves you 19 cents per year, forever, with zero volatility.

After that, rebuild your cash buffer. Aim for 3–6 months of living expenses in a high-interest savings account (HISA) or short-term GIC. In Canada in 2026, these are yielding 4–5% after inflation — not glamorous, but safe and liquid. Only then, with your debt gone and emergency fund intact, should you start investing.

When you do invest, skip the flashy microcap penny stocks. The fraud patterns you’ve seen — reverse splits, heavy dilution, hype without revenue — are traps for the eager. Instead, start with low-cost index funds: a broad Canadian equity index ETF (TSX Composite) or XUS (US total market). Simple. Broad. Cheap. And immune to pump-and-dump schemes.

This is an educational framework, not personalized financial advice.
